welcome: Welcome to my garage! I am Ustad. On the stand is a running single-cylinder engine, like the heart of many Royal Enfields. Drag to spin it, right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom. Every engine does one job: it turns small, controlled explosions into turning force.
anatomy: Let us take it apart. Slide to explode the engine, then click each part to learn its job. The piston slides in the cylinder, the connecting rod links it to the crankshaft, and the camshaft opens the valves. Find six parts to earn your first spanner.
fourstroke: This is the heartbeat: four strokes. Intake sucks in air and fuel. Compression squeezes it. The spark fires and power pushes the piston down. Exhaust blows the burnt gas out. Suck, squeeze, bang, blow. Press pause, scrub the crank, and notice it takes two full turns.
cams: Who opens the valves at exactly the right moment? The camshaft. A chain drives it from the crank through a sprocket twice as big, so the cam turns once for every two crank turns. Scrub the crank and watch the lobes push the valves. See where both are open together? That is overlap.
mixture: Fire needs the right recipe. About fourteen point seven parts air to one part petrol burns completely. Go lean and it runs hot. Go rich and it wastes fuel and smokes. Now time the spark: a little before top dead centre is best. Too early, and you hear knock.
twostroke: Some engines skip the valves. A two-stroke uses ports in the cylinder wall, and the piston itself opens and closes them. It fires on every turn, so it is light and punchy, but some fresh fuel escapes with the exhaust. Toggle the two and count the power pulses.
cooling: Burning fuel makes far more heat than motion, so it must go somewhere. A Classic 350 uses air and oil: fins shed heat into the wind. The Himalayan 450 is liquid cooled: a pump pushes coolant through the jacket to a radiator. Warm it up and watch the thermostat open.
oil: Oil is the engine's blood. A pump pulls it from the sump, pushes it through a filter, and sends it to the crank bearings, the cams and the cylinder walls. It forms a thin film so metal never touches metal, then drains back. Try draining the oil and watch the temperature climb.
breathing: Think of the engine as an air pump. Air enters through the air box and the throttle. Fuel comes from the tank through a pump to the injector. Burnt gas leaves through the header, the catalytic converter and the muffler. Twist the throttle and watch everything flow faster.
layouts: Now the family of engines. A single, a parallel twin, a V twin, a boxer, an inline three and an inline four. The layout changes the firing rhythm, the width, the vibration and the sound. Try the Interceptor's two-seventy twin, then press listen to hear each beat.
power: Torque is twist, the force on the crank. Power is how fast you deliver that twist, so power equals torque times rpm. Rev the engine and watch the numbers. Then shift gears: low gears multiply torque for pulling away, and high gears trade torque for speed.
dyno: Here are three real Royal Enfields. The Classic 350 is a long-stroke single that peaks early with lazy, thumping torque. The Himalayan 450 revs to eight thousand. The Interceptor 650 twin has the most torque of all. Hover the curves and compare.
lab: This is your Engine Lab. Pick any layout, set the speed, and switch between solid, x-ray and cutaway. Toggle the gas and flame, try liquid cooling, explode it, and click any part to name it. A good mechanic learns by tinkering.
quiz: Final inspection! Answer at least six of eight correctly and I will give you my own Ustad badge. Whatever happens, copy the cheat sheet. Every great mechanic keeps notes in the toolbox.
